query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the extent of chemical ordering in the Ni–Al–rich regions (which form Ni₃Al-like L1₂ domains) governs phase stability—in that highly ordered, stoichiometric domains raise the antiphase boundary energy and promote planar slip and strain localization (resulting in brittleness), whereas a controlled degree of off‐stoichiometric disorder lowers these barriers to cross‐slip and facilitates distributed deformation. This in turn sustains a balance of high‐temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance (via promotion of defect recombination sites), and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy exhibiting a dual-phase microstructure with a disordered FCC matrix and Ni–Al–rich regions that may form ordered intermetallic (L1₂) phases.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled annealing/tempering treatments to adjust the degree of chemical ordering in the Ni–Al–rich domains (for example, comparing aging treatments at ~600 °C versus ~750 °C).
generation.conditions: Samples processed under identical conditions except for the annealing temperature and/or time; mechanical testing performed over a range of temperatures (including cryogenic and high temperature) and radiation exposure in a controlled test environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, stoichiometry, and coherency of Ni₃Al‐like L1₂ domains within the disordered matrix and their interface quality.
generation.mechanism: A high degree of perfect ordering in the Ni–Al domains increases the antiphase boundary energy, leading to planar dislocation slip and localized strain (which fosters embrittlement and impairs toughness). In contrast, achieving a controlled, off‐stoichiometric, and slightly disordered ordering reduces the activation barrier for cross‐slip and promotes uniform deformation. This microstructural tuning thus allows the alloy to retain high-temperature strength, effective defect recombination (for radiation tolerance), robust oxidation/corrosion resistance, and sufficient cryogenic ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples annealed in the optimal temperature window (e.g., around 750 °C) will exhibit off‐stoichiometric, less perfect L1₂ domains that correlate with higher ductility, improved radiation damage tolerance, sustained high-temperature strength, and enhanced resistance to environmental degradation relative to samples annealed at lower temperatures (e.g., 600 °C) that show fully ordered, brittle Ni₃Al-like domains.
generation.baseline: The as-cast condition or samples aged at lower temperatures (e.g., ~600 °C) where strong, nearly perfect ordering results in pronounced L1₂ domains, leading to brittle fracture and less effective defect recombination.
generation.boundary: This mechanism operates in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys near the eutectic compositional ratios and under processing conditions that avoid excessive grain growth or formation of other deleterious secondary phases; its applicability to HEAs with significantly different compositions or processing histories remains to be established.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative correlations between the degree of ordering (e.g., measured APB energies, domain stoichiometry) and the full spectrum of properties such as radiation tolerance and cryogenic toughness still require further systematic investigation. It is also uncertain how irradiation exposure might interact with these ordered domains in long-term applications.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy samples and subject them to controlled annealing treatments at two different temperatures (e.g., 600 °C and 750 °C) designed to yield high versus moderated ordering in the Ni–Al–rich regions. Characterize the microstructure using TEM, atom probe tomography, and X-ray diffraction to quantify phases and ordering levels. Then, perform mechanical tests across a range of temperatures (including cryogenic and high-temperature regimes), conduct irradiation tests (to assess defect recombination efficacy), and evaluate corrosion/oxidation performance.
measurements: Degree of ordering and stoichiometry of the Ni₃Al-like L1₂ domains (using TEM/APT/XRD)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility) at room, high, and cryogenic temperatures
Radiation-induced defect densities and recombination rates
Environmental resistance via oxidation and corrosion tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples annealed at 750 °C do not exhibit a reduced degree of ordering (i.e., remain as ordered as the 600 °C sample) or if they do not demonstrate superior combinations of ductility, radiation tolerance, and environmental resistance compared to the 600 °C annealed samples, then the hypothesis that moderating chemical ordering in the Ni–Al–rich domains governs phase stability and balances the desired properties will be falsified.

System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) containing face-centered cubic (FCC) and ordered body-centered cubic (B2) phases. Processing: Vacuum induction levitation melting followed by isothermal aging at 520, 600, 700, 750, 800, 1000, and 1200 °C for 20 hours at a heating rate of 300 °C/h and rapid quenching in water.
